lessons.title: Why Chasing Loses — and How the Pullback Fixes It
lessons.summary: Explain why entering a trend on a pullback gives you a better price, a tighter stop and a clearer reason to be wrong than chasing the move.
lessons.html:
You have seen this happen, probably more than once. A pair starts trending. You notice it late, after a run of strong candles. It looks unstoppable, so you buy. Within a few hours price dips, your stop goes, and then — with you safely out — the trend carries on exactly as you expected.

The usual conclusion is "I was wrong". Usually you were not. Your read of direction was fine. What was wrong was the price you paid and the place you put your stop. You bought at the most stretched point of the move, and you placed your stop inside the market's normal breathing room.

This course is about fixing that. The trend pullback strategy is not clever. It does not predict tops or bottoms. It does one simple thing: it waits for a trending market to retreat, then joins the trend again when there is evidence the retreat is over. That waiting changes the entire geometry of the trade — the entry, the stop and the reward available — and it gives you a clean, objective reason to know when you are wrong.

The problem with chasing

Look at the first chart. The trend is obvious: a higher high, a higher low, then a powerful run of green candles. The chaser buys after that run, at the top of the leg.

Three things went wrong, and none of them was the direction.

First, the price was poor. After five or six strong candles, buyers who wanted in have mostly got in. The market is stretched away from its recent average price. Statistically, that is where short-term pullbacks start, not where they end.

Second, the stop had no meaning. The chaser put a stop roughly 40 pips below entry because 40 pips "felt reasonable". But there was nothing at that level — no swing low, no structure, nothing whose break would prove the trend had failed. The stop sat in empty space, inside the range a normal pullback was always likely to cover.

Third, the trade had no answer to the question "what would make me wrong?" The only honest invalidation level for this uptrend was the higher low far below. A stop there would have meant risking over 100 pips for an entry at the top of a leg. Either the stop is meaningless, or the risk is enormous. That is the chaser's trap.

KEY POINT

Chasing is rarely a direction mistake. It is a price-and-stop mistake.

The same trend, a better price

Now the same candles, traded differently. Nothing about the market has changed. The trader simply waited.

Price pulled back from the new high, as trends routinely do. It drifted lower for several candles, then printed a candle with a long lower wick — sellers pushed down, buyers pushed it back. The trader bought on the close of that candle and placed the stop a few pips beneath its low.

Notice what has happened to the trade.

  • The entry is lower. The trader bought roughly 30–40 pips below where the chaser bought, in the same trend.
  • The stop is meaningful. It sits below the low of the pullback. If price trades back through that low, the idea "the pullback has ended" is simply wrong — and the trader knows within a few candles.
  • The reward is larger relative to the risk. Because the stop is tight and the entry is low, the prior high alone is already worth more than the risk, and a target at three times the risk (3R) is within the trend's normal reach.

This is the whole case for the pullback, in one picture. Same market, same direction, completely different trade.

COMMON MISTAKE

Thinking a pullback entry means "buy any dip". It does not. A dip in a market with no trend is just a falling price. The strategy needs a trend first, a pullback second, and evidence the pullback has ended third — in that order.

Trends breathe

Why do pullbacks happen at all? Because trends are not straight lines. They move in a rhythm: a fast, strong leg in the trend's direction (the impulse), followed by a slower, smaller drift against it (the pullback, sometimes called a correction or retracement), followed by another impulse.

The impulse is the market moving with intent — large candles, mostly one colour, covering ground quickly. The pullback is the market catching its breath: earlier buyers taking profit, newer ones deciding where they want in. In a healthy uptrend, the pullback ends above the previous pullback low, and the next impulse takes price to a new high.

This rhythm is what the strategy exploits. We do nothing during the impulses — that is chasing. We watch during the pullbacks. We act only when the pullback appears to be ending and the next impulse appears to be starting.

The four questions

Every trade in this course comes from answering four questions, in order. A "no" at any stage means no trade.

  1. Is there a trend? Not "does it look like it's going up" — an objective answer, based on swing structure: higher highs and higher lows, or lower highs and lower lows. Module 1 makes this mechanical.
  2. Is this a pullback, or a reversal? A healthy pullback is slower, smaller and more hesitant than the impulse before it, and it holds the last higher low. A reversal looks different, and Module 2 shows you how.
  3. Has the pullback reached a sensible place? Pullbacks tend to end in a few recognisable areas: around the 20 or 50 EMA, at the old breakout level, or between 38% and 62% of the prior impulse. Ideally several of those agree.
  4. Is there evidence the pullback has ended? A rejection candle, or a break of the pullback's own small structure. We never buy simply because price has arrived somewhere. Module 3 covers triggers, stops and targets.

Sitting above all four is one more: does the higher timeframe agree? A one-hour pullback in the direction of the four-hour trend is a very different proposition from one fighting it.

Where this strategy does not work

Be clear about this from the start: the pullback strategy is a trend strategy. When there is no trend, it has nothing to offer.

In a range, price swings between a ceiling and a floor. The moving averages flatten and weave through the middle of the candles. Every drop towards the floor looks a little like a pullback; every bounce looks a little like a new trend. A trader who applies pullback rules here will take entry after entry that goes nowhere — small losses, again and again.

The strategy's most important skill is therefore refusing entries. Most of the time the four questions do not all come back "yes", so most of the time you do nothing. That is not a flaw. It is the point.

How this course is built

Module 1 makes the trend objective: swing structure, trend lines and moving-average filters. Module 2 dissects the pullback itself — healthy or not, and how deep. Module 3 covers execution: triggers, stops, targets, sizing and multi-timeframe alignment. Module 4 covers when not to trade, then hands you the complete playbook. Every chart is an illustrative training chart, not real market data, and nothing here is a signal to trade any market.

Going deeper

For experienced traders, the case for the pullback is really an argument about risk geometry and invalidation.

Every trade has a thesis — "this uptrend will continue" — and a point at which the thesis is proven wrong. For a trend, that point is structural: in an uptrend, the most recent confirmed higher low. The further your entry is from that point, the more you must risk to give the thesis room. Chasing maximises that distance. Pullback entries minimise it, because you are entering near the low of the pullback, which is close to the structure that would invalidate you.

The course uses two kinds of stop:

  • The trigger stop — beyond the low of the pullback itself. Tight, cheap, and invalidated if the pullback simply continues. This is the default.
  • The structural stop — beyond the last confirmed higher low of the trend. Wider, and invalidated only if the trend itself breaks. Useful when the pullback low and the trend's higher low are the same point.

A hypothetical illustration of why the geometry matters. Suppose two traders each risk 1% of their account per trade. Trader A chases and can realistically aim for 1R before the next pullback. Trader B enters on pullbacks and aims for 2.5R. With these purely hypothetical numbers, Trader A needs to be right more than half the time just to break even; Trader B breaks even at under 30%. Neither figure is a promise of anything — real results depend on execution, costs and the market — but the arithmetic shows why the entry location, not the direction call, is where much of the edge in trend trading tends to live.

Two warnings. First, waiting has a cost: some trends never pull back to a sensible level, and you will miss them. That is the fee for refusing bad prices, and you should accept it in advance. Second, the tight trigger stop will be hit more often than a wide structural stop. Losses are part of the method. The aim is for them to be small, planned and explainable.

Summary

  • Most chasing losses are a price-and-stop problem, not a direction problem.
  • Trends move in a rhythm of impulse and pullback; this strategy acts only as a pullback ends.
  • Every trade answers four questions in order: trend, pullback, location, evidence — plus higher-timeframe agreement.
  • A pullback entry puts the stop close to a level that genuinely proves you wrong, which makes larger rewards relative to risk realistic.
  • In a range there is no trend to pull back from, so the strategy stands aside.

quiz.q: A trader buys after six strong green candles and is stopped out before the trend continues higher. What was most likely wrong?
options: The direction call
The entry price and stop placement
The choice of currency pair
The timeframe was too high
quiz.why: The trend did continue, so the direction was right. Buying at the most stretched point of a leg, with a stop in empty space, is the chaser's real mistake.

quiz.q: In a healthy uptrend, what is a pullback?
options: Any red candle
A slower, smaller move against the trend that holds above the last higher low
A move that breaks the last higher low
A sideways range lasting several weeks
quiz.why: A pullback is the trend's breathing phase. If it breaks the last higher low, it is no longer an ordinary pullback.

quiz.q: Why does a pullback entry usually allow a larger reward relative to risk?
options: Pullbacks always reverse at exactly the 50 EMA
The stop can sit close to a level that genuinely invalidates the idea, while the target stays at the trend's next high or beyond
Brokers offer better spreads on pullbacks
Pullback trades never lose
quiz.why: Entering near the pullback low keeps the stop small and meaningful, while the trend's next leg is still available as the reward.

quiz.q: Which is the correct order of the strategy's four questions?
options: Trigger, location, trend, pullback
Trend, pullback, location, evidence
Location, trigger, trend, target
Evidence, trend, location, pullback
quiz.why: First establish a trend, then confirm it is a pullback rather than a reversal, then check location, then wait for evidence the pullback is ending.

quiz.q: Price is swinging between a clear ceiling and floor and the 20 and 50 EMAs are flat and crossing. What does the pullback trader do?
options: Buy every dip to the floor
Sell every rally to the ceiling
Stand aside — there is no trend to pull back from
Buy when price crosses above the 20 EMA
quiz.why: This is a range. Range trading is a different strategy; the pullback strategy needs a trend and has no business here.

lessons.title: The Only Trend Definition You Need
lessons.summary: Label swing highs and lows mechanically and classify any chart as uptrend, downtrend or no trend — the same way every time.
lessons.html:
Ask ten traders whether a chart is trending and you will get ten answers, most of them based on how the last few candles feel. That is no foundation for a strategy. If you cannot say objectively whether a trend exists, you cannot say objectively whether a pullback exists — and every decision after that is guesswork dressed as analysis.

This lesson gives you a definition you can apply to any chart, on any timeframe, and get the same answer as anyone else using the same rules. It is old — it goes back more than a century to Charles Dow — and it is still the best one available: a trend is a sequence of swings.

Swing highs and swing lows

Price does not move in straight lines. It zigzags. Each zig ends at a swing high — a peak with lower highs on both sides. Each zag ends at a swing low — a trough with higher lows on both sides.

To make this mechanical, use a simple rule: a candle is a swing high if its high is higher than the highs of the two candles before it and the two candles after it. A swing low is the mirror. This is sometimes called a five-candle fractal. It is not magic, and you can use three candles each side if you prefer fewer, larger swings. What matters is that you pick one rule and keep it.

Not every five-candle wiggle matters. A two-pip blip inside a strong leg technically qualifies but tells you nothing. So add a second filter: a swing only counts if the move away from it was meaningful — as a working guide, at least a third of the leg before it, or clearly visible when you zoom out to see the last 60–100 candles. If you have to squint to see it, it is not a swing for this strategy.

KEY POINT

Swings are the atoms of trend. Everything in this course — the trend, the pullback, the stop, the target — is defined by them.

The uptrend

An uptrend is a sequence of higher highs (HH) and higher lows (HL). Each rally makes a new high above the previous one. Each pullback ends above the previous pullback low.

Look at the lows in the chart. They step up: each sell-off runs out of sellers at a higher price than the last one did. That is the real signature of an uptrend. Highs get the attention, but the lows tell you that buyers are willing to pay more each time the market dips. Join those higher lows and you have the trend's floor.

You need at least two higher highs and two higher lows before calling something a trend. One higher high could be a bounce in a range. A second confirms a pattern.

The downtrend

A downtrend is the mirror: lower highs (LH) and lower lows (LL). Each sell-off makes a new low. Each rally fails below the previous rally high.

Here the important swings are the highs. Each bounce runs out of buyers at a lower price than the last. Sellers are prepared to sell earlier every time. The line through those lower highs is the ceiling, and a pullback trader in a downtrend is looking to sell rallies into that ceiling — the mirror image of everything we do in an uptrend.

Throughout this course, examples are mostly written for uptrends to keep the language simple. Every rule applies in reverse to downtrends: swap highs for lows, buy for sell, below for above.

When a higher low becomes official

Here is the subtle part, and the one most traders get wrong. While a pullback is happening, you do not yet know where its low is. Price might bounce from here, or it might keep going. So when is a higher low actually a higher low?

The answer: a pullback low is confirmed as a higher low only when price closes above the prior swing high.

Until that close, the low is a candidate. It might hold; it might not. The moment price closes above the prior high, two things become true at once: the uptrend has printed another higher high, and the low it launched from is now proven to be a level buyers defended. That low becomes the trend's current line in the sand.

This rule gives you something extremely valuable: an objective invalidation level at every point in the trend. At any moment, you can point to the last confirmed higher low and say "if price closes below there, the uptrend as I defined it is broken". That level will become central to your stops, your trade management and your decision about when the trend has ended.

COMMON MISTAKE

Moving your "line in the sand" down every time price falls through it. If the last confirmed higher low breaks on a closing basis, the uptrend is broken by definition. Redefining the trend to keep a position alive is how small losses become large ones.

No trend

The third state is the one beginners forget exists: no trend. If the swings contradict each other — a higher high followed by a lower low, a lower high followed by a higher low — there is no trend to follow.

This chart has a lot of movement and some large candles. It feels like it is going somewhere. But walk through the swings: a high, a low, a higher high, then a lower low that undercuts everything. Then a lower high. Then a higher low. Then a higher high. Every swing contradicts the one before. By definition, no trend exists, and the pullback strategy has nothing to join.

Markets spend a great deal of time in this state. Recognising it — and staying out — is as much a part of this strategy as any entry rule.

The state machine

Put it together and every chart, at every moment, is in exactly one of three states:

  • Uptrend — at least two HH and two HL, and the last confirmed HL has not been broken on a close. Permitted: long pullback trades only.
  • Downtrend — at least two LH and two LL, and the last confirmed LH has not been broken on a close. Permitted: short pullback trades only.
  • No trend — anything else, including the period straight after a trend breaks. Permitted: nothing.

Write the state down before you look for any trade. Write the invalidation level next to it. "EUR/USD H4: uptrend, last confirmed HL 1.0842." That one line, updated as new swings confirm, is the foundation of every trade in this course.

THE RULES
  • A swing high has lower highs on both sides (two candles each side); a swing low is the mirror.
  • Ignore swings created by moves too small to see on a 60–100 candle view.
  • Uptrend = at least two higher highs and two higher lows. Downtrend = at least two lower highs and two lower lows.
  • A pullback low becomes a confirmed higher low only when price closes above the prior swing high.
  • A close below the last confirmed higher low ends the uptrend. Anything that is not clearly up or down is "no trend".
  • Write down the state and the invalidation level before looking for a trade.

Going deeper

Closes, not wicks. Swing points are marked at the extreme of the wick, because that is where price actually traded. But breaks are judged on closes. A wick through the last higher low that closes back above it is a test, not a break. Intraday spikes through obvious swing levels are common, partly because that is where many stops cluster. Requiring a close on the timeframe you are analysing filters out much of that noise. You will occasionally be a candle late on a genuine break; that is a fair price.

Swing significance scales with the timeframe. A swing on the one-hour chart may be invisible on the daily. That is not a contradiction; it is magnification. A pair can be in a daily uptrend and a one-hour downtrend simultaneously, and both statements are correct. The answer is always to state your timeframe. Lesson 9 turns this into a working method.

Using volatility to filter swings. The "visible on a zoomed-out chart" filter is practical but subjective at the margins. A more mechanical version: a swing only counts if the move away from it covers at least one average true range (ATR) of the timeframe. Use whichever filter you can apply consistently.

The awkward middle. After an uptrend breaks, the chart is in "no trend" until a downtrend has its own credentials — a lower high and a lower low. That gap can last a long time, and it is where many traders lose money by insisting on a verdict the market has not given. The state machine forces you to sit on your hands until it has.

Sloppy swings. Real charts throw up double bottoms, inside candles and swings that differ by a pip. Treat two lows within a few pips of each other as the same swing. When in genuine doubt, the honest label is "no trend" — doubt itself is information.

Summary

  • A trend is a sequence of swings: HH and HL for an uptrend, LH and LL for a downtrend.
  • Mark swings with a fixed rule and ignore the tiny ones.
  • A pullback low only becomes a confirmed higher low when price closes above the prior high.
  • The last confirmed higher low is the trend's invalidation level; a close below it ends the uptrend.
  • Contradictory swings mean no trend — and no trade.

quiz.q: What objectively defines an uptrend in this course?
options: Price above the 200 EMA
At least two higher highs and two higher lows
Three green candles in a row
RSI above 50
quiz.why: Indicators can support the read, but the definition is structural: a sequence of higher highs and higher lows.

quiz.q: Price pulls back and bounces from a low. When does that low become a confirmed higher low?
options: As soon as a green candle prints
When the RSI turns up
When price closes above the prior swing high
When it touches the 20 EMA
quiz.why: Until price closes above the prior high, the low is only a candidate. The close proves the trend continued from that low.

quiz.q: In an uptrend, the last confirmed higher low is broken by a long wick, but the candle closes back above it. What is the correct read?
options: The uptrend is over
A downtrend has started
The level was tested, not broken — the uptrend is intact
The higher low should be moved lower
quiz.why: Breaks are judged on closes. A wick through the level that closes back above is a test.

quiz.q: A chart shows a higher high, then a lower low, then a lower high. What state is it in?
options: Uptrend
Downtrend
No trend
Uptrend in a deep pullback
quiz.why: One lower low and one lower high is not yet two of each, and the earlier higher high contradicts them. Mixed swings mean no trend.

quiz.q: Why does the strategy need to know the last confirmed higher low at all times?
options: It is the only place you can enter
It is the objective level that, if closed below, ends the uptrend
Brokers require it
It is always the profit target
quiz.why: It is the trend's invalidation level — the basis for stops, management and deciding when the trend has ended.

lessons.title: Trend Lines Drawn Properly
lessons.summary: Draw trend lines and channels by fixed rules, validate them with a third touch, and know what a broken line does and does not tell you.
lessons.html:
The trend line is the most used and most abused tool in charting. Open a typical beginner's chart and you will find a web of lines at every angle, each drawn to justify a feeling and quietly redrawn the moment price breaks it. That is not analysis. It is decoration.

Used properly, though, a trend line is genuinely helpful to a pullback trader. It shows the trend's pace at a glance, marks where pullbacks have tended to end, and gives early warning when the pace changes. This lesson gives you the rules for a line worth keeping — and puts the line in its proper place, which is second to swing structure.

The hierarchy: structure first, lines second

Lesson 2 defined the trend by swings: higher highs and higher lows. That definition is primary. A trend line is merely a way of visualising the pace of those swings.

So when a trend line and swing structure disagree, structure wins. Every time. Most trend-line mistakes come from promoting the line above the structure it was meant to summarise — exiting a healthy trend because a line was touched, or holding a broken trend because a generously redrawn line has not been.

KEY POINT

A trend line summarises the trend. It does not define it. Swings define it.

Five rules for a line worth keeping

Rule 1 — Connect confirmed swing points. An uptrend line runs beneath the market through swing lows. A downtrend line runs above it through swing highs. Use swings that are already confirmed by Lesson 2's rules. If you cannot say which two swings your line connects, delete it.

Rule 2 — Two points draw a line; a third validates it. Any two points can be joined. That proves nothing. The line becomes meaningful only when a later pullback comes back and respects it. Until then it is a hypothesis in pencil.

In this chart the line is anchored on swing lows 1 and 2. On its own, that line could be anything. Then the third pullback drifts down, touches the line and turns higher. Now the line has history: three separate sell-offs have run out of sellers at the same rising slope.

Rule 3 — Pick a convention and keep it. Wicks or bodies? Traders argue about this endlessly. The honest answer is that either works if you are consistent and neither works if you switch whenever it flatters you. This course anchors on wicks. Treat the line as a zone a few pips wide, not a laser. Price does not owe your line precision.

Rule 4 — Never redraw to rescue a broken line. If price closes decisively through a validated line, that line's job is done. You may draw a new line that reflects the trend's new pace, but you may not pretend the break did not happen.

Rule 5 — Respect what the slope tells you. The angle of the line is the speed of the trend. A near-vertical line drawn during a euphoric run will break almost by arithmetic, because no market sustains that pace. Its break usually means "pace normalising", not "trend over". A gentle line that has held for many touches is a different matter; its break is more serious.

A broken line is not a broken trend

The most common trend-line error is treating any break as a reversal signal. Look at what actually happened here.

The first line was drawn under a fast early run. When the pace slowed, price slipped beneath it almost immediately. A trader who treats lines as signals would have sold, or exited a long. But check the structure: the pullback that broke the line ended above the previous higher low. No swing was broken. The trend simply slowed down, and a new, gentler line took over.

So when a line breaks, ask one question: has the last confirmed higher low broken on a close? If not, the trend is intact and decelerating. Pay attention, note it, but do not act as though the trend has ended. If the higher low also breaks, you have a structural break, and the line merely gave you a few candles' early notice — which is exactly the job of a secondary tool.

COMMON MISTAKE

Drawing the steepest possible line through the first two lows of a fast move and then treating its break as a sell signal. Steep lines break because pace normalises. Check structure before concluding anything.

Channels

Copy a validated trend line and place the copy across the swing highs, and you have a channel.

When price genuinely respects both rails, the channel is a picture of the trend's whole rhythm. For a pullback trader it does two practical jobs:

  • The lower rail marks where pullbacks have habitually ended. That is an area of interest for entries — not a trigger on its own, but a place to start watching closely.
  • The upper rail marks where impulses have tended to pause. That is useful when setting a realistic target. If the upper rail is 40 pips above your entry and your target is 120 pips away, you are asking the trend to do something it has not done recently.

Two cautions. Clean channels are rarer than textbooks suggest; if you are stretching tolerance on every touch to keep the picture alive, there is no channel. And watch for changes: a market that can no longer reach its upper rail is losing momentum, while one that bursts out of the top is often in an unsustainable final spurt.

Trend lines in downtrends

Everything mirrors. A downtrend line runs across the lower highs, and rallies into it are the downtrend's pullbacks — the places a pullback trader looks to sell.

Two lower highs anchor the line. The third rally drifts up into it, stalls, and prints a bearish rejection candle with a long upper wick. The short is taken on that candle's close, with the stop above the wick and a target at twice the risk. Notice the line did not create the trade on its own. It marked where to pay attention; the rejection candle provided the evidence.

How the pullback trader actually uses lines

In this strategy, trend lines do three jobs and no others:

  1. Locating pullbacks. A validated line, or the lower rail of a channel, is one of the areas where pullbacks often end. It joins the moving averages and prior structure covered in Lesson 6 as a possible point of confluence.
  2. Early warning. A break of a well-established line means the trend's pace has changed. Tighten attention, consider tightening management, and check structure.
  3. Triggers inside the pullback. A pullback often forms its own small counter-trend line. When price breaks back through that small line, it is evidence the pullback is ending. Lesson 7 builds this into a full entry trigger.
THE RULES
  • Swing structure defines the trend; trend lines only summarise it. When they disagree, structure wins.
  • Anchor lines on confirmed swing points: lows for uptrends, highs for downtrends.
  • A line is a hypothesis until a third touch respects it.
  • Choose wicks or bodies once and keep the convention. Treat the line as a zone a few pips wide.
  • Never redraw a line to rescue a position. A decisive close through a validated line is a break; log it.
  • A line touch is a place to watch, never a trade on its own.

Going deeper

Why lines work at all. There is nothing mystical here. A validated trend line marks the rate at which buyers have been willing to pay up. Each touch is a moment where the market's pace of acceptance and the pullback's selling ran into each other. Many participants see the same obvious line, which adds some self-fulfilling attention. Equally, many traders' stops sit just beyond it, which is why lines are often briefly pierced before price recovers. Use closes, not wicks, for breaks.

The trend-line fan. Mature trends often step through several lines, each shallower than the last: steep, then moderate, then gentle. Each break is a deceleration. A third break of a fan, especially with a structural break, is a strong sign the trend is ending. This is a useful way to see late-trend exhaustion without any indicator.

Acceleration lines. The opposite also happens: a trend breaks out of the top of its channel and steepens. That is not automatically good news. Parabolic acceleration is often the trend's final phase, and pullbacks from it can be sharp. A pullback trader is more cautious, not less, after an acceleration.

Do not over-fit. On any chart, with enough freedom, you can find a line through three points. That is why the anchor points must be confirmed swings chosen in advance, and why validation must come from a later touch, not from scanning back for a third point that happens to line up.

Timeframes. A line drawn on the four-hour chart is more meaningful than one drawn on the five-minute chart, for the same reason that higher-timeframe swings are more significant. When you show a line to yourself as evidence, say which timeframe it came from.

Summary

  • Trend lines summarise swing structure; structure always has the final say.
  • Anchor on confirmed swings, validate with a third touch, keep one convention, never redraw to rescue a trade.
  • A broken line means the pace has changed; only a broken higher low means the trend has broken.
  • Channels show where pullbacks usually end and where legs usually pause — helpful for targets.
  • Lines tell you where to look. Candles tell you whether to act.

quiz.q: How many touches does a trend line need before it is considered validated?
options: One
Two
Three — two to draw it, a later third to validate it
Five
quiz.why: Any two points make a line. A later third touch that respects the line is what gives it meaning.

quiz.q: A steep trend line breaks, but the pullback holds above the last confirmed higher low. What is the correct read?
options: The trend has reversed — go short
The trend has slowed but is structurally intact
Redraw the line through the new low
The trend line was drawn on the wrong timeframe
quiz.why: Structure decides. A broken line with an intact higher low means the pace has changed, not the trend.

quiz.q: Which swing points anchor a downtrend line?
options: Swing lows
Swing highs
Candle closes only
Any two candles
quiz.why: A downtrend line runs across the lower highs, above price.

quiz.q: Price touches the lower rail of a clean up-channel. What should the pullback trader do?
options: Buy immediately at the rail
Start watching for a trigger — the rail is an area of interest, not a signal
Sell, because the channel will break
Move the rail to fit the latest low
quiz.why: Lines mark where to pay attention. Entries need evidence, such as a rejection candle or a break of the pullback's own structure.

quiz.q: A trader's validated line breaks, so they redraw it through the latest low to keep their long position 'valid'. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing — lines should always be updated
It rescues a position instead of analysing the market; a decisive break of a validated line should be logged as a break
They should have used bodies instead of wicks
Lines can only be drawn on the daily chart
quiz.why: You may draw a new line for a new pace, but never to pretend a break did not happen.

quiz.q: On a channel, the upper rail is 40 pips above a planned entry and the target is 130 pips away. What does this suggest?
options: The target is conservative
The target asks the trend to do more than it has recently done — consider a nearer target or skip
The channel is invalid
The stop must be widened
quiz.why: The upper rail shows where legs have tended to pause. A target far beyond it is optimistic for this trend's rhythm.

lessons.title: Moving Averages as Trend Filters
lessons.summary: Use the 20, 50 and 200 EMAs to grant or refuse permission to trade, and recognise the flat, braided averages that mean stand aside.
lessons.html:
Moving averages are usually sold as signal generators: buy when the fast line crosses the slow one, sell when it crosses back. Used that way, they are late, noisy and expensive in sideways markets. Used as a filter, they are one of the most useful tools a pullback trader has.

A filter does not tell you when to trade. It tells you when you are allowed to. It sorts the market into "trend I can trade", "trend in the other direction" and "nothing worth trading", and then it throws away every setup that does not fit. Nobody screenshots the trade a filter stopped them taking, but over hundreds of trades those refusals are a large part of what keeps a trend strategy healthy.

What a moving average actually tells you

A moving average is the average closing price over a set number of candles. The exponential moving average (EMA) gives more weight to recent candles, so it turns a little faster than the simple moving average (SMA). For a filter, the difference is minor. This course uses EMAs throughout for consistency.

Three things about an average matter to a pullback trader:

  • Where price is relative to it. Price above a rising average means recent prices are higher than the average of the period — buyers are in control of that window.
  • Its slope. A rising average says the trend has persisted long enough to drag the average up. A flat average says the market has gone nowhere over the period, whatever the last few candles look like.
  • How two averages relate. A faster average above a slower one says recent prices are higher than older prices. That is a crude but robust definition of an uptrend.

None of these is a timing tool. All of them are good at describing the regime.

The working pair: 20 and 50 EMA

The core filter in this course uses the 20 EMA and 50 EMA on your trading timeframe. A market qualifies for long pullback trades only when all of the following are true:

  1. Price is above the 50 EMA (it may dip to or slightly through the 20 during a pullback).
  2. The 20 EMA is above the 50 EMA.
  3. Both averages are visibly sloping upward.
  4. Swing structure agrees: higher highs and higher lows, as defined in Lesson 2.

When you see this picture — price above both, the averages stacked in order, both rising, swings stepping up — the filter is open for longs. Mirror everything for shorts: price below the 50, the 20 below the 50, both sloping down, lower highs and lower lows.

Notice that the fourth condition is structure. The averages do not replace Lesson 2; they confirm it. If the averages say "uptrend" but the swings say "no trend", the answer is no trend. Structure has the final word, exactly as it did with trend lines.

KEY POINT

The averages grant permission. Structure confirms it. A trigger candle is still required. All three, or no trade.

The slow filter: the 200 EMA

Above the working pair sits an optional slow filter: the 200 EMA. It is a regime label, not a trading line.

While price holds above a rising 200 EMA, the pullback trader only considers longs. Below a falling 200 EMA, only shorts. When price is tangled around a flat 200, many traders either stand aside or reduce size.

You do not need both the 200 EMA and a higher-timeframe check (Lesson 9). They usually say the same thing. Choose one regime filter and use it consistently; stacking three filters that all measure the same trend just means paying three tolls for one road.

What "no" looks like

The single most valuable thing the filter does is say no. Here is what that looks like.

The 20 and 50 EMAs are flat and keep crossing. Price swings above and below them. This is the environment in which moving-average strategies bleed: every cross looks, up close, like the start of a trend, and almost none follows through. In a range the average settles into the middle of the oscillation, which means price crosses it constantly — exactly where trend tools are waiting.

The signs to watch for:

  • Flat slope. The 50 EMA moving sideways is the market telling you, in its own language, that there is no consensus to follow.
  • Braiding. One cross of the 20 and 50 is information. Several crosses in a short period is a range.
  • Contradictory swings. Higher highs mixed with lower lows, as in Lesson 2.
  • Your own results. Two consecutive stop-outs from the same setup on the same pair is your strategy reporting, accurately, that its assumptions do not currently hold.
COMMON MISTAKE

Taking a beautiful trigger candle in a market the filter has already disqualified. The filter is not paperwork. It is the strategy.

The ten-second filter routine

Run the same routine on every chart, in the same order, before you look at a single candle pattern:

  1. Slope of the 50 EMA. Up, down or flat? Flat ends the routine: no trade.
  2. Order of the averages. Is the 20 on the correct side of the 50 for that slope? If the 50 is rising but the 20 has dropped below it, the market is mid-transition. No trade yet.
  3. Price location. Is price on the correct side of the 50? A pullback may dip into or slightly through the 20; a candle closing well beyond the 50 against the trend is a warning you will meet again in Lesson 6.
  4. Swings. Do the last two highs and lows agree with the averages? If not, structure overrules them.

Write the result as one line: "H1 EUR/USD — filter open, longs only" or "filter closed". Doing it the same way every time matters more than doing it cleverly. A routine that takes ten seconds and is applied without exception will protect you better than an elaborate one you skip when the chart looks exciting.

Practice drill

Work through the filter before you reveal the answer. Check slope, order of the averages and swing structure — in that order — and only then look at the candle.

Now compare it with the same kind of candle in a market that passes every check.

The candle shape is almost identical. The verdict is opposite, because the context is opposite. In the first chart the pin bar is just one more swing in a range. In the second it is a rejection at the 20 EMA inside a qualified uptrend, with higher lows beneath it and both averages rising. The pattern is the sentence; the trend is the paragraph it appears in.

THE RULES
  • Longs only when: price above the 50 EMA, 20 EMA above 50 EMA, both sloping up, and swings making higher highs and higher lows.
  • Shorts only when: price below the 50 EMA, 20 EMA below 50 EMA, both sloping down, and swings making lower highs and lower lows.
  • Flat or braided averages mean no trade, however good the candle looks.
  • Optional regime filter: trade only in the direction of the 200 EMA's slope. Use one regime filter, not several.
  • Averages are never entry signals on their own. They permit; triggers act.

Going deeper

Quantifying slope. "Visibly sloping" is fine for most traders, but if you want a mechanical test, compare the 50 EMA now with its value 10 candles ago. If the change is smaller than roughly one-third of an average candle range per 10 bars, call it flat. The exact threshold matters less than applying the same one every time. Test it on historical charts, then freeze it.

Lag is the price of smoothness. A 20-period EMA reflects, roughly, the last 10 to 20 candles; a 50 EMA, the last 25 to 50. That lag is why averages are poor at timing and good at describing. By the time the 20 crosses the 50, the move is not new. That is fine for a filter, because the pullback strategy never tries to catch the first leg of a trend. It waits for the trend to prove itself and then joins the second, third and fourth legs.

Timeframe matters. A 200 EMA on the five-minute chart describes about 17 hours of trading. That is a regime in the way a weekend is an era. Apply the slow filter on a timeframe where 200 candles represents weeks, not hours, or use the higher-timeframe method from Lesson 9 instead.

Filters cost something. A good filter typically means fewer trades and shallower losing streaks, because the worst streaks in most trend systems come from repeatedly trading against a strong trend or through a range. But the filter will also veto some trades that would have worked, including the occasional spectacular reversal. That is the wager: across many trades, the vetoed group is expected to do worse than the trades you keep. Whether that holds for your exact rules is a measurement you make by testing, not an article of faith.

Settings. The 20/50 pair is a sensible default, not scripture. Faster markets sometimes suit 9/21; slower approaches, 50/100. Choose in testing, then stop tuning. Adjusting settings after every losing week until the recent past looks good is curve-fitting, and it produces a system that perfectly describes last month and nothing else.

Summary

  • Moving averages are filters: they grant or refuse permission; they do not time entries.
  • Longs need price above the 50, the 20 above the 50, both rising, and structure agreeing. Mirror for shorts.
  • The 200 EMA, or a higher-timeframe check, can serve as a slow regime filter. Use one, not several.
  • Flat, braided averages and contradictory swings mean stand aside.
  • The same candle can be a good trade or a bad one. Context decides.

quiz.q: In this course, what is the main job of the 20 and 50 EMAs?
options: To generate buy and sell signals when they cross
To grant or refuse permission to trade in a direction
To set exact profit targets
To predict reversals
quiz.why: They filter the market into tradeable and untradeable regimes. Entries come from triggers, not from the averages.

quiz.q: Which situation qualifies for long pullback trades?
options: Price above the 20 EMA, 20 EMA below the 50 EMA
Price above both, 20 above 50, both rising, higher highs and higher lows
Price below a falling 50 EMA
Averages flat but price just crossed above them
quiz.why: All four conditions — position, order, slope and structure — must pass.

quiz.q: The 20 and 50 EMAs have crossed five times in the last 60 candles and both are flat. A perfect bullish pin bar prints at the 20 EMA. What do you do?
options: Buy — the candle is textbook
Buy with half size
No trade — the filter has already disqualified this market
Sell, because ranges always fall
quiz.why: Flat, braided averages describe a range. A good candle does not rescue a failed filter.

quiz.q: Why might using the 200 EMA, a higher-timeframe 50 EMA and a 100 SMA together as filters be a poor idea?
options: They are illegal to combine
They usually measure the same trend, so they add complexity and cost without adding much new information
The 200 EMA only works on gold
Filters should never be used
quiz.why: Stacked filters that agree with each other are paying three tolls for one road. Choose one regime filter.

quiz.q: What is the cost of using a trend filter?
options: There is no cost
It vetoes some trades that would have won, including occasional big reversals
It always increases the number of trades
It makes stops wider
quiz.why: A filter's wager is that the trades it removes would, as a group, do worse than those it keeps. Some good trades are lost along the way.

lessons.title: Healthy Pullback or Start of a Reversal?
lessons.summary: Judge a pullback by its speed, size and character, and tell an ordinary breather from a counter-move that is breaking the trend.
lessons.html:
Every trend spends a large part of its life retreating. Count the candles in a healthy uptrend and a surprising share of them are red. So the question you will face more than any other as a pullback trader is this: is this retreat an ordinary pullback, or the beginning of the end?

Get it right and you buy into a trend at a good price. Get it wrong and you are buying something that is falling for a reason — catching the first leg of a new downtrend and calling it a discount.

This lesson gives you two ways to answer the question. The first is character: how the pullback is travelling. It gives early, imperfect warnings. The second is structure: whether the last confirmed higher low holds. It gives a late, definitive verdict. You need both.

Impulse and correction

Trends move in two distinct ways. Impulses travel with intent: large candles, mostly one colour, covering ground quickly. Corrections — pullbacks — drift: smaller candles, mixed colours, overlapping each other, moving gently against the trend.

In a healthy trend, the impulses point with the trend and the corrections point against it. The strong moves and the structure agree. That is what "healthy" means.

Read the chart as a pair of legs. The impulse covered about 100 pips in eight candles, almost all green and large. The pullback took eighteen candles to give back well under half of that, in small candles of both colours, each overlapping the last. That is the signature of profit-taking, not of sellers taking control. Buyers are still the dominant side; they are just pausing.

Three things to measure

You do not need an indicator to judge a pullback. Compare it with the impulse before it on three measures.

1. Speed. How many candles did the pullback take compared with the impulse? A healthy pullback is usually slower — it takes as long or longer to cover less ground. A pullback that covers the same ground as the impulse in fewer candles is faster than the trend. That is a warning.

2. Size. How much of the impulse has been given back? A typical healthy pullback retraces roughly a third to two-thirds of the prior leg. A pullback that has given back the entire leg and more is no longer a pullback by any useful definition. Lesson 6 turns this into precise zones.

3. Character. What do the candles look like? Healthy pullbacks are overlapping and mixed: small red candles interrupted by green ones, wicks on both sides, a sense of reluctance. A pullback made of large, consecutive red candles with small wicks — candles that look like an impulse — is a market where sellers are acting with conviction.

KEY POINT

A healthy pullback is slower, smaller and messier than the impulse it follows. When the counter-move is faster, larger and cleaner than the trend, be suspicious.

When the counter-move out-muscles the trend

Here is what the alternative looks like.

The trend had printed a new higher high. Then, instead of drifting, price fell. Six large red candles undid the entire last rally — faster and with bigger bodies than anything the buyers had produced. It sliced through both averages, and then a candle closed below the last confirmed higher low.

At that point there is nothing left to debate. The character warned first: the biggest candles on the chart now point down. Structure then confirmed it: the higher low has broken on a close, and by Lesson 2's definition the uptrend is over. The next rally stalled below the old low, forming the first lower high. A trader who bought this "pullback" at the 20 EMA, or at the 50, was buying into the first leg of a new move against them.

COMMON MISTAKE

Treating any fall into a moving average as a pullback. A pullback is defined by how price arrives, not just where. Price falling hard into the 50 EMA is not the same as price drifting into it.

Rhythm as early warning

Character can deteriorate long before structure breaks. Watch the rhythm of the whole trend, not just the latest pullback.

Every low in this chart is still higher than the last; by the rules, this is an uptrend. But look at the legs: +130 pips, then +95, then +70. Each impulse is shorter than the one before. And the pullbacks have grown: -35, then -60, then -60 again. The trend is tiring. Buyers are reaching less far each time, and sellers are taking back more.

Fading rhythm does not end a trend. Plenty of trends slow down, digest for a while, and then resume strongly. But it should change your behaviour:

  • Be more demanding about entries. Require stronger triggers and better confluence.
  • Be more modest with targets. If the last leg was 70 pips, a target 150 pips away is asking for a lot.
  • Watch the last confirmed higher low closely. It is now the line that matters most.

Think of it this way: rhythm is the warning light; structure is the red card. Rhythm makes you defensive. Only structure makes you stop trading the trend.

Practice drill

Decide before you reveal. The uptrend is intact on paper. What does the way price arrived tell you?

A simple pullback scorecard

Before you look for a trigger, score the pullback on four questions:

  1. Has it taken more candles than the impulse did? (yes = healthy)
  2. Has it given back less than about two-thirds of the impulse? (yes = healthy)
  3. Is it made of small, mixed, overlapping candles? (yes = healthy)
  4. Is it holding above the last confirmed higher low on a closing basis? (yes = required)

Question 4 is a requirement: if it fails, the trade is off. Questions 1 to 3 are a judgement. Three healthy answers: proceed to location and trigger. Two: proceed only with excellent confluence. One or none: the pullback is behaving like a reversal, and the strategy waits for it to prove otherwise.

THE RULES
  • A pullback must hold above the last confirmed higher low on a closing basis. A close below ends the trade idea.
  • Judge every pullback against the impulse before it: speed, size and character.
  • A counter-move with larger, faster candles than the trend is a warning, even if structure has not broken yet.
  • Shrinking impulses and deepening pullbacks mean be defensive: stricter entries, modest targets.
  • Price arriving at a moving average is not a pullback by itself. How it arrived matters.

Going deeper

Why corrections overlap. In an impulse, one side is in a hurry: orders arrive faster than the other side cares to absorb them, so candles close near their extremes and barely overlap. In a correction, the dominant side has paused but not left. Early buyers take profit, newer buyers bid on dips, and the result is choppy, two-way trade. Overlap is the visible footprint of that two-way trade. A correction with no overlap is not two-way trade; it is one-way selling.

Measuring "faster". A practical, mechanical comparison: divide each leg's size in pips by the number of candles it took. If the pullback's pips-per-candle is more than the impulse's, the pullback is faster than the trend. For a stricter test, compare the average body size of the pullback candles with the average body size of the impulse candles.

Complex pullbacks. Not every pullback is one smooth drift. Many take an A-B-C shape: a dip, a small bounce that fails below the high, and a second dip that often reaches a little lower. Traders who buy the first dip are often stopped by the second. If the first dip ends shallow and fast, expect the possibility of a second leg, and let the trigger rules in Lesson 7 decide when the pullback is truly over.

Exhaustion versus reversal. A tiring trend and a reversing trend are different things. Exhaustion is the trend losing energy. Reversal requires a new trend in the opposite direction with its own credentials — a lower high and a lower low. Between the two there is often a long, choppy no-man's-land. Lesson 10 covers it in detail. For now: fading rhythm means fewer, better trades; broken structure means no trades on that side.

The one-candle trap. Traders often treat the first green candle after a sharp decline as proof the pullback has ended. One small candle against a run of large ones is not evidence of anything except a pause. The trigger rules later in the course demand a candle that actually rejects the level, or a break of the pullback's own structure — not just a change of colour.

Summary

  • Every pullback is judged by speed, size and character, compared with the impulse before it.
  • Healthy pullbacks are slower, smaller and more overlapping than the impulse.
  • A counter-move that is faster and stronger than the trend is a warning; a close below the last confirmed higher low is the verdict.
  • Fading rhythm — shorter legs, deeper pullbacks — means be defensive, not that the trend has ended.
  • How price arrives at a level matters as much as the level itself.

quiz.q: An impulse rose 120 pips in 10 candles. The pullback has fallen 45 pips over 16 small, mixed candles and holds above the last higher low. How does it score?
options: Unhealthy — it took too long
Healthy — slower, smaller and overlapping
A reversal — it has fallen more than 30 pips
Impossible to judge without RSI
quiz.why: Slower than the impulse, well under two-thirds of it, and made of mixed candles: textbook healthy behaviour.

quiz.q: Which pullback characteristic is the strongest warning?
options: Small candles of both colours
A pullback that takes longer than the impulse
Large, consecutive red candles that fall faster than the rally rose
A pullback that stops at the 20 EMA
quiz.why: When the counter-move is faster and stronger than the trend, sellers are acting with conviction.

quiz.q: Impulses have shrunk from 130 to 95 to 70 pips while pullbacks have grown, but every low is still higher. What is the correct stance?
options: The trend is over — go short
The trend is intact but tiring — be more selective and modest with targets
Nothing has changed
Double position size because the trend is mature
quiz.why: Rhythm is the warning; structure is the verdict. Fading rhythm calls for defence, not reversal.

quiz.q: Which of the scorecard questions is a hard requirement rather than a judgement?
options: The pullback took more candles than the impulse
The pullback candles overlap
The pullback holds above the last confirmed higher low on a closing basis
The pullback reached the 50 EMA
quiz.why: If the higher low breaks on a close, the uptrend is over by definition and the trade idea is void.

quiz.q: After a sharp, six-candle decline into the higher low, one small green candle closes. Is that enough evidence the pullback has ended?
options: Yes — any green candle is a trigger
No — one small candle after a run of large ones is a pause, not proof
Yes, if it is above the 50 EMA
Only on a Friday
quiz.why: The trigger rules require a genuine rejection or a structural break of the pullback, not a change of colour.

lessons.title: How Deep Is a Normal Pullback?
lessons.summary: Mark the zone where a pullback is most likely to end by stacking the 20/50 EMAs, prior structure and the 38–62% retracement — and recognise when a pullback has gone too deep to trust.
lessons.html:
You now know how to tell a healthy pullback from a reversal. The next question is the one every pullback trader asks while watching price drift against the trend: where is this likely to stop?

Nobody knows exactly. Anyone who tells you a pullback "will" end at 61.8% is selling something. But pullbacks are not random either. In a trending market they tend to end in a small number of recognisable areas, for reasons that have more to do with how traders behave than with any magic in the numbers. If you can mark those areas in advance, you stop reacting to every red candle and start waiting in the right place.

This lesson gives you three tools for measuring depth — moving averages, prior structure and retracement percentages — and one principle for combining them: confluence. A zone where two or three tools agree is worth waiting at. A level that only one tool likes is a suggestion, not a plan.

Tool one: the moving-average band

Lesson 4 used the 20 and 50 EMAs as a filter. They also make an excellent depth gauge, because they move with the trend. A fixed horizontal level from a week ago may be miles away by now; the averages are always where the market's recent "fair price" sits.

Think of the space between the 20 and the 50 as a band:

  • Shallow pullbacks touch or barely pierce the 20 EMA. These are typical of strong, fast trends where buyers are impatient.
  • Normal pullbacks reach into the band between the 20 and the 50.
  • Deep pullbacks test the 50 itself, and occasionally close slightly through it before recovering.

A pullback that closes decisively beyond the 50 against the trend — several candles, not a single wick — is no longer behaving like an ordinary pullback. It is not automatically a reversal, but it has moved into the territory Lesson 5 warned about, and the burden of proof shifts.

The point of that chart is not that the 20 EMA is special. It is that the depth of pullbacks tells you about the trend's strength. Fast trends pull back shallowly. Mature, tiring trends pull back deeply. You adjust where you wait to the trend you actually have.

Tool two: prior structure

The second tool is older than any indicator: broken resistance tends to become support (and broken support tends to become resistance in a downtrend).

When an uptrend makes a new high, it breaks through the previous high. That old high was a level where sellers once won. Once price has cleared it, traders who missed the breakout often place orders to buy if it comes back; traders who sold there and were proven wrong may buy back to close their positions near their entry. Whatever the mix of motives, the observable result is that pullbacks very often pause at or near the old breakout level.

On a chart, this is simple to mark. Find the swing high the current impulse broke through. Draw a line or a narrow zone at that level. If the pullback reaches it, you are at prior structure.

Two practical notes:

  • Treat it as a zone, not a laser line. Price may undershoot or overshoot by a few pips; on H1 for major pairs, a zone of 8–15 pips is sensible.
  • The most useful structure is the most recent broken level. A level from three swings ago is history.

Tool three: the retracement percentage

The third tool measures the pullback as a fraction of the impulse before it. Draw a retracement from the impulse's low to its high (in an uptrend). A pullback that gives back a third of the leg has retraced about 33%. One that gives back half has retraced 50%.

Most charting platforms label this tool "Fibonacci" and draw levels at 23.6%, 38.2%, 50%, 61.8% and 78.6%. You do not need to believe anything mystical about those ratios. What matters is the rough bands they describe:

  • Under 38% — shallow. Common in strong trends; matches the 20 EMA zone.
  • 38% to 62% — the normal range for a healthy pullback. Most of your setups will form here.
  • 62% to 79% — deep. Still possible in a healthy trend, but the higher low is getting close and the reward to the prior high is shrinking.
  • Beyond 79% — the pullback has erased almost the whole leg. The trend's last higher low is under threat and the setup should be treated as suspect.
KEY POINT

Depth is measured against the impulse that preceded the pullback, not against the whole trend.

Confluence: where the tools agree

Each tool on its own is weak. Moving averages are approximate. Prior structure is a zone, not a line. Retracement percentages are bands, not levels. But when two or three of them point at the same area, that area becomes a genuinely good place to watch.

Here is the process, every time:

  1. Mark the impulse. Identify the low and high of the most recent leg in the trend's direction.
  2. Shade the 38–62% band of that impulse.
  3. Mark the most recent broken swing level — the old high the impulse broke through.
  4. Note where the 20 and 50 EMAs are right now, and where they will roughly be in a few candles' time (they are rising in an uptrend).
  5. Look for the overlap. The area where at least two of these coincide is your pullback zone. Write down its upper and lower edge.

Notice what the confluence does and does not do. It tells you where to pay attention. It does not tell you to buy. Price arriving in a zone is a reason to watch, not a reason to act — Lesson 7 covers the evidence you need before entering. In the chart above, the entry comes only after a candle has pushed into the zone and been rejected out of it.

COMMON MISTAKE

Placing a limit order at the 61.8% level and walking away. Pullbacks overshoot. A limit order fills on the way down, before any sign the pullback has ended — which is exactly the moment the strategy is designed to avoid.

Practice drill

When the pullback goes too deep

The bands also tell you when to lose interest. A pullback that keeps going beyond about 79% of the impulse has given back almost everything the trend gained on its last leg. Several things are now true at once:

  • The last higher low is close, so any stop beyond it gives you very little room before structure breaks.
  • The reward to the prior high is no longer comfortably larger than the risk — because the prior high is now a long way above you, but so is any sensible confirmation.
  • The character of the move has usually changed: the counter-move is starting to look like an impulse itself.

That chart shows the price of ignoring depth. A trader who bought the bounce because "it is still above the higher low" was technically correct for a few candles, and then was not. Depth beyond 79% is not a rule that the trend has ended; it is a rule that this setup has become poor value, and poor value is reason enough to skip.

A worked depth plan

Here is the routine applied to a hypothetical H1 chart on EUR/USD, so you can see the numbers.

  • Last impulse: low 1.0880, high 1.1000 — 120 pips.
  • 38.2% retracement: 1.0954. 61.8% retracement: 1.0926.
  • Old high broken by the impulse: 1.0935.
  • 50 EMA currently near 1.0930 and rising about 1 pip per candle.
  • Last confirmed higher low: 1.0880.

The overlap of the 38–62% band, the old high and the 50 EMA is roughly 1.0926 to 1.0940. That is the pullback zone. The trader writes it down, sets a price alert at the top edge and does nothing until price gets there. If price arrives and prints a rejection candle, a trigger stop under that candle's low might sit around 1.0915 — still 35 pips above the higher low, which leaves a sensible margin. The prior high is 60–70 pips above a typical entry. With 20–25 pips of risk, that is roughly 2.5–3R to the first target before the trend even makes a new high.

If, instead, price slices through the zone and down to 1.0890, the plan is simple: the zone has failed, the higher low is 10 pips away, and the setup is skipped.

Going deeper

Why these levels "work" at all. There is no evidence that markets know about Fibonacci. What the 38–62% band captures is simply where pullbacks in a trend tend to cluster: big enough to shake out late buyers, small enough to leave the structure intact. Many traders watch the same levels, which may add a small self-fulfilling effect, but you should treat the levels as a description of typical behaviour, not a law. That is also why we insist on a zone and a trigger rather than a precise level.

Depth and expectancy trade off. Waiting only for deep pullbacks gives better prices and larger reward-to-risk ratios, but you will miss most strong trends, which rarely pull back that far. Accepting shallow pullbacks catches more trends but at worse prices with tighter margins. Neither is right. A sensible compromise is to let the trend's own recent rhythm decide: if the last two pullbacks stopped at the 20 EMA, expect the next to do something similar; if they reached the 50, wait for the 50.

Measuring from the right points. Always measure the impulse from the swing low that started it to the extreme of the high — wicks included, consistently. Measuring from a random intra-leg low makes every pullback look deeper than it is. If the impulse is unclear, the setup is probably unclear too.

Higher-timeframe overlap. The strongest pullback zones often coincide with a level from the timeframe above — the 20 EMA on H4 sitting in the same place as the 50 EMA on H1, for example. Lesson 9 shows how to look for that without drowning in lines.

Downtrends. Everything here mirrors exactly. Measure the impulse from its high to its low, shade the 38–62% band above the low, mark the old low that was broken (now likely resistance), and watch the 20 and 50 EMAs from below.

THE RULES
  • Measure depth against the most recent impulse, from its swing low to its swing high (or high to low in a downtrend).
  • Define a pullback zone where at least two of these overlap: the 20–50 EMA band, the most recent broken swing level, the 38–62% retracement.
  • Arrival in the zone is never an entry on its own — wait for a trigger (Lesson 7).
  • A pullback beyond roughly 79% of the impulse, or closing decisively beyond the 50 EMA, is treated as suspect and normally skipped.

Summary

  • Pullbacks tend to end in a few recognisable places: the 20–50 EMA band, the most recent broken swing level, and the 38–62% retracement of the prior impulse.
  • Shallow pullbacks signal a strong trend; deep pullbacks signal a tiring one. Let the trend's own rhythm guide where you wait.
  • A zone where two or three tools overlap is where you pay attention — but you still need evidence before you enter.
  • Beyond about 79% the setup becomes poor value: the higher low is too close and the trend's character is changing.
  • Everything mirrors for downtrends.

quiz.q: An impulse runs from 1.2600 to 1.2720. Roughly where is the 50% retracement?
quiz.why: The impulse is 120 pips; half of that is 60 pips; 1.2720 minus 60 pips is 1.2660.

quiz.q: What does a series of very shallow pullbacks that only touch the 20 EMA usually tell you?
options: The trend is weak
The trend is strong and buyers are impatient
A reversal is imminent
The 20 EMA is broken
quiz.why: Shallow pullbacks are typical of strong trends. Insisting on a 50–62% retracement in that kind of trend usually means never getting in.

quiz.q: Which combination best describes a high-quality pullback zone?
options: A single 61.8% level
The old broken high, the 50 EMA and the 38–62% band overlapping
Any round number
Wherever the RSI reaches 30
quiz.why: Confluence — two or three independent tools pointing at the same area — is what makes a zone worth waiting at.

quiz.q: Price has just entered your pullback zone on a large red candle. What do you do?
options: Buy immediately — it's in the zone
Place a limit order at the bottom of the zone
Wait for evidence the pullback has ended, such as a rejection candle
Sell, because the candle is red
quiz.why: The zone tells you where to watch. Entry requires a trigger. Arrival on a strong red candle is often followed by an overshoot.

quiz.q: A pullback has retraced 85% of the prior impulse and is now trading below the 50 EMA. How should the pullback trader treat it?
options: As the best possible entry, because the price is so low
As suspect — the higher low is close and the trend's character is changing
As proof the trend has reversed
As a reason to widen the stop to 200 pips
quiz.why: Beyond about 79% the setup becomes poor value. It is not proof of reversal — that needs the higher low to break — but it is reason enough to skip.

lessons.title: Entry Triggers — Evidence the Pullback Is Over
lessons.summary: Use rejection candles and breaks of the pullback's own structure to time entries, so you buy after the pullback shows signs of ending rather than while it is still falling.
lessons.html:
You have a trend. You have a healthy pullback. Price has arrived in a zone where the moving averages, the old breakout level and the 38–62% retracement agree. This is the moment most traders press the button.

It is also the moment this strategy asks you to wait a little longer.

Arrival is not evidence. A pullback that reaches your zone may stop there, or it may slice through it, or it may pause for three candles and then fall another 40 pips. You cannot tell which from the arrival alone. What you need is evidence that the pullback has ended — something on the chart that shows the counter-trend move losing its grip and the trend reasserting itself.

This lesson gives you two kinds of evidence, called triggers: the rejection candle, and the break of the pullback's structure. You need one of them, in the right place, before you enter. Without one, there is no trade, however good the zone looks.

Why wait for a trigger at all?

Because a trigger converts a guess into a test.

Without a trigger, your stop has to go somewhere arbitrary below the zone, and the market can keep falling into it with nothing to tell you the pullback is still alive. With a trigger, you have a specific candle or a specific swing that says "the pullback ended here". Your stop goes just beyond it. If price trades back through that point, the evidence has been contradicted and you are out — quickly, and for a small, known loss.

There is a cost. Waiting for a trigger means entering a little higher than the very bottom of the pullback. You will never buy the exact low. That is fine. The extra few pips buy you a much better-defined reason to be in the trade, and they filter out a large share of pullbacks that were never going to hold.

KEY POINT

The zone says where to look. The trigger says when to act. You need both.

Trigger one: the rejection candle

A rejection candle shows, within a single bar, that price pushed into the zone and was pushed back out. In an uptrend you are looking for a candle that trades down into the zone and closes back up near its high. There are two common shapes.

The pin bar. A candle with a long lower wick — at least twice the length of its body — and a close in the upper third of its range. The wick is the visible trace of sellers pushing price down and failing to keep it there. For our purposes the body colour matters less than where it closes: a pin bar closing near its high is a pin bar whether its body is green or slightly red.

The engulfing candle. A bullish candle whose body completely covers the body of the red candle before it. It shows buyers not merely holding the line but taking back everything sellers achieved in the previous bar — and more.

What makes a rejection candle valid for this strategy:

  1. Location. It forms inside your pullback zone, or its wick reaches into it. A beautiful pin bar in the middle of nowhere is just a candle.
  2. Size. It is at least average size for recent candles. A tiny pin bar on a quiet hour tells you very little.
  3. Close. It closes in the trend's direction — in the upper third of its range for longs, the lower third for shorts.
  4. Context. The pullback has the character of a pullback: slower and smaller than the impulse, and the last higher low is intact.

The entry is simple: enter at the close of the trigger candle (or, if you prefer slightly more confirmation, on a break of its high in the next candle — at the cost of a slightly worse price). The stop goes a few pips beyond the candle's wick. Lesson 8 refines exactly how far.

The same idea in a downtrend

Everything mirrors. In a downtrend you are looking for a candle that rallies up into the zone and closes back down near its low — a bearish pin bar with a long upper wick, or a bearish engulfing candle that swallows the green candle before it.

COMMON MISTAKE

Treating any candle with a wick as a pin bar. A pin bar's wick must be long relative to its body and to recent candles, and it must close near the opposite end. A candle with two wicks and a small body in the middle is indecision, not rejection.

Trigger two: break of the pullback's structure

Not every pullback ends with a dramatic candle. Many end quietly. Price drifts down in a gentle staircase of lower highs and lower lows — a miniature downtrend inside the bigger uptrend — then stops making lower lows, and finally pushes back up through the last small lower high.

That push is your second trigger. Remember Lesson 2's definition of a trend: a sequence of swings. A pullback in an uptrend is a small downtrend. When that small downtrend breaks its own structure — when price closes above its most recent lower high — the pullback has ended by the same objective rules you use for trends.

There are two ways to mark it:

  • Small swing high. Mark the most recent lower high inside the pullback. A candle closing above it is the trigger.
  • Counter-trend line. Draw a line across the pullback's lower highs, as Lesson 3 described. A candle closing decisively above that line is the trigger.

They usually give the same signal within a candle or two. Use whichever is clearer on the chart in front of you.

The structure-break trigger has one clear advantage: it often comes with a stronger confirmation, because by the time the pullback's line breaks, price has already moved off its low. It also has one clear disadvantage: the entry is higher and the stop, which still belongs beneath the pullback low, is therefore wider. Expect a smaller R multiple to the prior high than with a well-placed pin bar. Run the numbers each time; if the prior high is less than about 1.5R away, the setup is not worth taking.

Losing trades with good triggers

Here is the uncomfortable part. A valid trigger in a valid zone, in a valid trend, still fails a meaningful share of the time. Nothing on a chart prevents that.

Look at what the trigger did here. It got the trader in at a sensible price, with a stop exactly where the idea "the pullback ended at this candle" was disproved. When price fell through the wick, the trader was out within a few candles, for a planned 1R loss — long before the trend's higher low broke and the pullback turned into a reversal. Without the trigger discipline, that same trader might have bought earlier, with no meaningful stop, and ridden the whole collapse.

The aim of a trigger is not to win every time. It is to make every loss small and explainable, so that the winners — which run to the prior high and beyond — can pay for them.

Practice drill

Choosing between the two triggers

You do not need to prefer one trigger in every situation. A useful rule of thumb:

  • When the pullback ends with a sharp spike into the zone, a rejection candle is the natural trigger. Waiting for the pullback's structure to break would put your entry too far from the low.
  • When the pullback is a slow, orderly drift, the structure break is usually cleaner. Slow drifts produce few dramatic candles, and the pin bars that do appear are often small and unconvincing.

Whichever you use, write it down in advance. "If a rejection candle closes in the zone, I buy its close. If price drifts through the zone without one, I will buy a close above the pullback line, provided the prior high is still at least 1.5R away." A trader with a written plan does not invent triggers in the moment.

Going deeper

Close versus intrabar. Every trigger in this course is judged on a closed candle. A pin bar that is forming looks perfect until the last five minutes, when price drops and turns it into an ordinary red candle. If you trade from an H1 or H4 chart, set an alert for the candle close and decide then.

Entry refinements. Experienced traders sometimes enter on a 50% retracement of the trigger candle itself, using a limit order, to improve the price. It does improve the R multiple when it fills. It also misses the strongest moves, which never look back. If you use it, test it on your own records and be honest about the trades it skips.

Trigger on a lower timeframe. You can look for the trigger on a lower timeframe than the one that defines the trend — for example, an H4 trend and zone, with the trigger taken from the H1 chart. This often gives a tighter stop. It also gives more false triggers. Lesson 9 covers this alignment properly.

What the trigger does not do. A trigger is not a forecast. It is a small, observable fact — the pullback was rejected here — and the trade is a bet that this small fact is the start of the next impulse. Treat it with the respect a small fact deserves: one candle cannot outweigh a broken structure, a range or a higher timeframe pointing the other way.

Hypothetical expectancy. Suppose, purely for illustration, a trader takes 100 trades with an average win of 2.2R and an average loss of 1R. At a 35% win rate, the expectancy is 0.35 × 2.2 − 0.65 × 1 = 0.12R per trade. At 30% it is −0.04R. These are invented numbers, not a forecast, but they show how much depends on the R multiple — which is why the trigger's job of keeping the stop tight matters so much.

THE RULES
  • No trigger, no trade: arrival in the zone is never enough on its own.
  • Valid triggers: a rejection candle (pin bar or engulfing) closing in the trend direction from inside the zone, or a close beyond the pullback's own last swing or counter-trend line.
  • Judge every trigger on a closed candle.
  • Enter on the trigger's close; stop a few pips beyond the trigger candle or the pullback extreme.
  • If the first target is less than about 1.5R away, skip the trade.

Summary

  • A trigger is evidence the pullback has ended; without one there is no trade.
  • Rejection candles — pin bars and engulfings — show price being pushed into the zone and rejected out of it, within one bar.
  • A close beyond the pullback's own small structure or counter-trend line is the second trigger, cleaner after slow drifts.
  • Valid triggers still lose. Their purpose is to make every loss small, early and explainable.
  • Judge triggers on closed candles, write your trigger rules down in advance, and skip anything under about 1.5R to the first target.

quiz.q: Price has just reached a strong pullback zone. Why does the strategy still wait for a trigger?
options: Because zones never hold
Because arrival gives no evidence the pullback has ended and no logical place for a tight stop
Because brokers require confirmation
To make sure the trade is a winner
quiz.why: A trigger provides both the evidence and the precise point at which that evidence is disproved — which is where the stop goes.

quiz.q: Which candle is a valid bullish pin bar for this strategy?
options: A small candle with equal wicks above and below
A candle in the zone with a lower wick over twice its body, closing in the upper third of its range
Any green candle at the 50 EMA
