A large red candle with a long upper wick
quiz.why: Long lower wick, close near the high, inside the zone. Equal wicks show indecision, not rejection.

quiz.q: When is a structure-break trigger usually the better choice?
options: After a sharp spike into the zone
After a slow, orderly drift with few decisive candles
Only on Mondays
When the trend has already ended
quiz.why: Slow drifts rarely produce convincing rejection candles. A close above the pullback's own line or last lower high is cleaner.

quiz.q: A valid pin bar trade is stopped out for 1R. What does this tell you about the trigger?
options: Pin bars do not work
Nothing on its own — valid triggers lose regularly; the trigger kept the loss small and early
The stop should have been 100 pips wider
The trader should double size next time
quiz.why: No trigger guarantees a win. Its purpose is a small, defined loss when wrong, so winners can pay for losers over many trades.

quiz.q: A forming H1 candle looks like a perfect pin bar with ten minutes left. What should you do?
options: Enter now to get a better price
Wait for the candle to close and judge it then
Enter half now and half later
Move to the M1 chart and enter there
quiz.why: Triggers are judged on closed candles. Many 'perfect' pin bars change shape in the final minutes.

quiz.q: After a structure-break trigger, the prior high is only 1.2R away. What do you do?
options: Take it anyway — the trigger is valid
Skip it — the reward to the first obstacle is too small
Move the stop closer until it is 2R
Remove the target
quiz.why: A valid trigger with poor reward is still a poor trade. Moving the stop to manufacture R puts it in meaningless space.

lessons.title: Stops, Targets and Position Size
lessons.summary: Place stops beyond the swing that proves you wrong, choose targets from prior highs, measured moves or fixed R multiples, and size every trade so a loss costs a planned fraction of your account.
lessons.html:
Most traders spend ninety per cent of their effort on entries and ten per cent on everything else. It should probably be the other way round. A mediocre entry with a well-placed stop, a sensible target and the right position size can still make a sound trade. A brilliant entry with a stop in the wrong place, a target picked from thin air and a position that is too large will eventually hurt you, however good the trigger looked.

This lesson covers the three numbers every pullback trade needs before you enter: where you are wrong (the stop), where you will take profit (the target), and how much you trade (the position size). They are not afterthoughts. They decide whether the trade is worth taking at all.

The stop goes where the idea is wrong

A stop is not a pain threshold. It is not "the most I can bear to lose". It is the price at which the reason for the trade has been disproved by the market. Everything else follows from that.

For a pullback trade, the idea is: the pullback ended at this point, and the trend is resuming. So the stop belongs just beyond the point where the pullback ended. There are two versions, which Lesson 1 introduced.

The trigger stop. A few pips beyond the extreme of the trigger candle or the pullback low — whichever is further. If price trades back through it, the evidence that the pullback ended has been contradicted. This is the default for this course: tight, cheap and quick to tell you when you are wrong.

The structural stop. Beyond the last confirmed higher low of the trend (or lower high in a downtrend). If price trades there, the trend itself is broken. It is wider, so the position must be smaller, but it is hit less often. It suits traders who cannot watch the market closely, and setups where the pullback low and the trend's higher low are close together anyway.

Whichever you choose, add a buffer. Price often overshoots a level by a few pips — a spread widening, an order being filled, a wick running stops — before turning. Placing your stop exactly on the low invites that. A buffer of 2–5 pips on H1 majors, or about 10–20% of the average candle range, is a sensible starting point. On gold or yen pairs, measure the buffer in the same proportion rather than the same number of pips.

KEY POINT

The stop marks the price where the market proves your idea wrong — not the amount you are comfortable losing.

The stop in empty space

The most common stop mistake is not a stop that is too wide. It is a stop that is placed for convenience — "15 pips feels right" — in a spot that means nothing.

That trader did not lose because the analysis was wrong. They lost because the stop was placed where the market routinely goes during a perfectly healthy continuation. If the logical stop makes the trade too expensive, the answer is a smaller position, not a closer stop. If even a small position cannot make the numbers work, the answer is to skip the trade.

COMMON MISTAKE

Moving the stop closer to make the R multiple look better. It does make the number look better — right up until an ordinary wick takes you out of a trade that was going to work.

Targets: three ways to take profit

A pullback trade has three natural targets. You can use one, or combine them.

1. The prior high. The extreme of the impulse before the pullback (in an uptrend). This is the first obstacle: price has turned there before, and some sellers will be waiting. It is the most conservative target and the one this course uses as the first target and the minimum test of a trade: if the prior high is not at least 1.5R away, the trade is skipped.

2. The measured move. Trends often produce legs of similar size. Measure the previous impulse — say 110 pips — and project the same distance from the pullback low. It gives a sensible estimate of where the next leg might reach if the trend's rhythm continues. Treat it as a likely area, not a promise.

3. A fixed R multiple. A target at, say, 2R or 3R regardless of chart levels. It is mechanical and easy to test, and it stops you agonising over levels. Its weakness is that it ignores structure: a 3R target placed just beyond a major prior high may be harder to reach than the same target with clear space above it.

Combining targets

A practical, widely used approach is to split the position:

  • Close half at the prior high (T1).
  • Move the stop on the remainder to breakeven or to just below the trigger candle's low.
  • Let the remainder run to the measured move or 3R, or trail it behind new higher lows.

Splitting smooths your results: you bank something on many trades and still let a few run. The cost is that, on the trades that run cleanly to 3R, you will have made less than a trader who held the full position. There is no free lunch; choose a method and use it consistently so your records mean something.

Trailing the stop behind structure

Once a trade is well in profit, the same logic that placed your first stop can manage the rest. In an uptrend, each new confirmed higher low is a new level where the trend would be proven wrong. Move the stop to just beneath each new higher low as it is confirmed, and never move it backwards.

Trailing behind structure captures the big trends that occasionally run much further than any fixed target. It also gives back a meaningful chunk at the end, because the stop sits below the last higher low, not at the top. That is the price of letting winners run.

When there is no room: the trade you skip

Targets are not only for exits. They are a filter. Before entering, measure the distance from entry to the first obstacle — usually the prior high — and divide by the distance to your stop.

This is a hard rule to follow, because the trade in that chart worked. But a plan that takes 0.5R trades will need to win two out of every three of them merely to break even. Over enough trades, poor ratios drain an account even when the reading of the trend is good.

Position size: the number that keeps you in the game

Every trade in this course is sized by risk, not by lots or by feel. Decide in advance what fraction of your account you will lose if the stop is hit — illustratively 0.5% to 1% — and let the stop distance determine the size.

A worked example with illustrative figures:

  • Account: £10,000. Risk per trade: 1% = £100.
  • Stop distance: 24 pips (the trigger stop in the first chart).
  • Illustrative pip value on EUR/USD: about £7.50 per pip for one standard lot (it varies with exchange rates and your account currency — check your platform).
  • Size = £100 ÷ (24 × £7.50) = 0.56 lots.

Now use the structural stop instead: 70 pips. Size = £100 ÷ (70 × £7.50) = 0.19 lots. Same £100 at risk; a much smaller position. That is the whole point: the stop decides where you are wrong, and the size decides how much being wrong costs. Change one and the other must change with it.

Keep risk per trade constant across all setups, however confident you feel. Losing streaks happen to every method. At 1% per trade, ten losses in a row costs about 10% of the account — painful, survivable. At 5% per trade, the same streak costs about 40%, and the maths of recovering from that is brutal.

Going deeper

Breakeven stops. Moving the stop to breakeven early feels safe and often costs money: it converts many trades that would have dipped and then won into scratch trades. A common compromise is to move to breakeven only after T1 is hit, or after a new higher low has formed above entry.

Volatility-scaled buffers. Fixed pip buffers behave differently in quiet and busy conditions. Using a fraction of the Average True Range (for example 0.2 × ATR(14)) keeps the buffer proportional to how much the market is currently moving.

Expectancy, hypothetically. Imagine — with invented numbers — that a trader's pullback trades win 40% of the time and lose 60%. If every winner is closed at 2R and every loser costs 1R, expectancy is 0.4 × 2 − 0.6 × 1 = +0.2R per trade. If the same trader starts accepting 1R targets, expectancy becomes 0.4 × 1 − 0.6 = −0.2R, even though the entries are identical. That is why the 1.5R minimum is a rule rather than a preference.

Gaps and slippage. A stop is an instruction, not a guarantee. Over weekends or around major data releases, price can jump past a stop and fill worse. Size so that an occasional fill at 1.5R does not change your plans.

THE RULES
  • The stop goes beyond the point that disproves the trade — the trigger extreme or the last swing — plus a small buffer. Never in empty space.
  • If the logical stop is too far, trade smaller or skip. Never move the stop closer to improve the ratio.
  • The first target is the prior high (or low). If it is less than about 1.5R away, skip the trade.
  • Size every trade so a stop-out costs the same planned fraction of the account (illustratively 0.5–1%).
  • Stops move only in the trade's favour.

Summary

  • Stops mark where the market proves the trade wrong: beyond the trigger (default) or beyond the last swing (structural), with a small buffer.
  • A stop in empty space, or inside the trigger's own wick, is the most common way to lose on a correct read.
  • Targets: prior high first, then a measured move, fixed R multiple or trailing stop behind new swings.
  • The distance to the first obstacle is a filter — under about 1.5R, skip.
  • Position size comes from the stop distance and a fixed fraction of the account, so every loss costs the same.

quiz.q: Where does the default stop go in this strategy?
options: A fixed 20 pips below entry
A few pips beyond the trigger candle's extreme or the pullback low
At the 200 EMA
Wherever keeps the loss under £50
quiz.why: The trigger stop sits where the evidence that the pullback ended would be contradicted, plus a small buffer.

quiz.q: The logical stop for a setup is 60 pips away, which is more than you would like. What is the correct response?
options: Move the stop to 25 pips
Reduce position size so the risk stays at your planned percentage, or skip
Double the position to make it worthwhile
Remove the stop
quiz.why: Stop placement comes from the chart; size adjusts to fit it. If the numbers still do not work, the trade is skipped.

quiz.q: An impulse measured 120 pips. The pullback low is at 1.2700. Where is the measured-move target?
quiz.why: Project the impulse length from the pullback low: 1.2700 + 120 pips = 1.2820.

quiz.q: Entry 1.0950, stop 1.0920, prior high 1.0980. Should you take the trade?
options: Yes — the trigger is valid
No — the prior high is only 1R away, below the 1.5R minimum
Yes, but move the stop to 1.0940
Only with double size
quiz.why: 30 pips of risk and 30 pips to the first obstacle is 1R. Under the 1.5R minimum, the trade is skipped.

quiz.q: Account £8,000, risk 1%, stop 40 pips, illustrative pip value £8 per lot. What size?
options: 2.5 lots
0.25 lots
1 lot
0.08 lots

quiz.q: In a running long trade, a new higher low has been confirmed above your current stop. What does the trailing method do?
options: Leaves the stop where it is
Raises the stop to just below the new higher low
Moves the stop to the entry candle
Closes the trade

lessons.title: Multi-Timeframe Alignment
lessons.summary: Use a higher timeframe to define the trend and the pullback zone, a lower timeframe to time the trigger, and stand aside when the two disagree.
lessons.html:
Here is a puzzle that catches almost every trader at some point. On the one-hour chart, a pair is in a clean uptrend: higher highs, higher lows, the 20 EMA above a rising 50. You buy a textbook pullback. Within a day you are stopped out, and when you finally zoom out to the four-hour chart, you see why: the whole one-hour "uptrend" was a single pullback inside a four-hour downtrend, and you bought it just as it reached the level where the bigger trend resumed.

Nothing was wrong with your one-hour analysis. It was simply the wrong question. A trend exists on a particular timeframe, and the same market can trend up on one and down on another at the same moment. Lesson 2 noted this as a matter of magnification. This lesson turns it into a working method.

One market, several magnifications

Think of timeframes as zoom levels on the same map. The daily chart shows the motorway. The four-hour chart shows the junctions. The one-hour chart shows the individual lanes. A car changing lanes on the motorway is still travelling in the motorway's direction — unless it is taking an exit.

For a pullback trader, the useful structure is this:

  • The higher timeframe defines the trend and the zone. It answers: which way is the market trending, and where is the current pullback likely to end?
  • The lower timeframe times the trigger. It answers: has the pullback ended yet, and where exactly does my stop go?

A pullback on the higher timeframe is, by definition, a small trend in the opposite direction on the lower timeframe. When the higher-timeframe pullback ends, the lower timeframe shows it as a trend change — the counter-trend structure breaks, and the lower timeframe swings back into line with the higher one. That moment, inside the higher-timeframe zone, is the entry.

Choosing your pair of timeframes

Use a ratio of roughly four to six between them. Common pairings:

  • Daily trend, H4 trigger — swing traders checking twice a day.
  • H4 trend, H1 trigger — part-time traders checking several times a day.
  • H1 trend, M15 trigger — traders who can watch a full session.

Too close a ratio (H1 and M30) and the two charts tell you the same thing. Too wide (daily and M5) and the lower timeframe is so noisy that most "triggers" are meaningless.

KEY POINT

The higher timeframe decides whether and where. The lower timeframe decides when.

The top-down routine

Step 1 — Higher timeframe: trend. Apply Lessons 2 and 4. Higher highs and higher lows? 20 EMA above a rising 50? If not, stop here.

Step 2 — Higher timeframe: pullback and zone. Is the current move against the trend a healthy pullback (Lesson 5)? Mark the zone (Lesson 6): the EMA band, the old breakout level and the 38–62% band of the last impulse.

Step 3 — Lower timeframe: wait. Drop to the lower timeframe only when price is in or near the higher-timeframe zone. On the lower chart, the pullback will look like a downtrend: lower highs, lower lows, often a clean counter-trend line.

Step 4 — Lower timeframe: trigger. Wait for that small downtrend to break: a close above its last lower high or its counter-trend line, or a decisive rejection candle at the zone (Lesson 7).

Step 5 — Stop and target. Stop beyond the lower-timeframe pullback low (usually tighter than anything the higher timeframe could offer). First target: the higher-timeframe prior high.

Notice the stop. On the H4 chart, the only obvious stop would be below a four-hour candle's low or below the H4 higher low — wide, and expensive. On the H1 chart, the pullback low is close to the entry. The higher timeframe gave the direction and the target; the lower timeframe gave a precise trigger and a tighter stop. That combination is the main practical benefit of working across timeframes.

When the timeframes disagree

The other benefit is defensive. Most of the trades that multi-timeframe analysis improves are the ones it removes.

The rule is simple: only take lower-timeframe triggers in the direction of the higher-timeframe trend. When the higher timeframe is trending down, lower-timeframe buy signals are counter-trend trades, however tidy they look. When the higher timeframe has no trend — a range, or the tangle of flat averages from Lesson 4 — the strategy has no direction to align with, and you stand aside on both timeframes.

There are three possible states, and only one of them is a green light:

  1. Aligned. Higher timeframe trending; lower timeframe pulling back and then breaking back into line. Trade.
  2. Opposed. Higher timeframe trending the other way. No trade in the lower timeframe's direction. If anything, the lower-timeframe rally is the higher timeframe's pullback — a potential setup in the higher timeframe's direction later.
  3. Undefined. Higher timeframe ranging or ambiguous. No trade.
COMMON MISTAKE

Looking at the higher timeframe only after taking a lower-timeframe trade, to find reasons it will work. The higher timeframe is step one, not a second opinion.

Levels from the timeframe above

Sometimes the higher-timeframe trend is fine, but a major level from that timeframe sits right in the way.

This is where many traders over-complicate things. You do not need to check six timeframes. A quick look at the next timeframe up from your trend timeframe — the daily, if you trade H4 — for one thing only: is there a major level between my entry and my target? If there is, either use it as the target or skip the trade if that leaves less than 1.5R.

A worked top-down example

Illustrative numbers on GBP/USD, trading H4 and H1:

  • Daily: price in an uptrend; no major resistance until well above 1.2950.
  • H4: higher highs and higher lows; 20 EMA above a rising 50. Last impulse 1.2722 to 1.2860. The 50% level is 1.2791; the 50 EMA is near 1.2795; the old high from before the impulse is about 1.2785. H4 zone: 1.2780–1.2805.
  • H1: price enters the zone in a staircase of lower highs. The trader draws the line across them and sets an alert. Several hours later an H1 candle closes at 1.2801, above the line and above the last lower high at 1.2795.
  • Stop: below the H1 pullback low of 1.2780, with a buffer: 1.2776. Risk 25 pips.
  • Target: H4 prior high at 1.2860, 59 pips away: about 2.4R. Comfortably above the 1.5R minimum.
  • Size: 1% of the account divided by 25 pips' worth of pip value (Lesson 8).

Every number in that plan was decided before the trigger candle closed. The trader's only job at that point was to check the close against the line and press the button — or not.

Going deeper

Why alignment helps. When a higher-timeframe pullback ends, traders on several timeframes tend to be acting in the same direction at roughly the same time: higher-timeframe traders buying their zone, lower-timeframe traders buying their structure break. The observable result is that aligned triggers often move away from the entry faster. That is a tendency, not a law, and it is one reason the tight lower-timeframe stop is affordable.

The cost of alignment. You will take fewer trades. Some lower-timeframe trends that run strongly against the higher timeframe will be missed — occasionally that is the start of a new higher-timeframe trend, and you will be late to it. Accept that in exchange for avoiding the much more common case: buying the top of a higher-timeframe pullback.

Do not over-stack. Two timeframes, plus a glance at a third for major levels, is enough. Requiring daily, H4, H1 and M15 all to agree will leave you with almost no trades, and the few left will often be late. If you use the 200 EMA as a regime filter (Lesson 4), you may not need the third timeframe at all; they measure much the same thing.

When the trigger timeframe's trend changes first. Sometimes the lower timeframe forms a clean new uptrend while the higher-timeframe pullback has not reached the zone — a shallow pullback. In a strong higher-timeframe trend, this can be acceptable if the reward to the prior high still exceeds 1.5R. In a weaker trend, wait for the zone.

THE RULES
  • Define trend and pullback zone on the higher timeframe first. No higher-timeframe trend, no trade.
  • Take triggers only on the lower timeframe, only inside or near the higher-timeframe zone, and only in the higher timeframe's direction.
  • Use a timeframe ratio of roughly four to six (D1/H4, H4/H1, H1/M15).
  • Check the next timeframe up for a major level between entry and target; if it leaves less than 1.5R, skip.

Summary

  • A trend belongs to a timeframe; the same market can trend in opposite directions on different ones.
  • The higher timeframe decides whether to trade and where the zone is. The lower timeframe decides when, and gives a tighter stop.
  • A higher-timeframe pullback ends as a lower-timeframe trend change inside the zone — that is the entry.
  • When the timeframes disagree, there is no trade. When the higher timeframe is ranging, there is no trade.
  • Glance one timeframe higher for major levels in the way; do not stack more timeframes than you need.

lessons.title: When the Trend Ends — and Ranges Where the Strategy Fails
lessons.summary: Recognise the structure break that ends a trend, avoid buying "pullbacks" in a market that has stopped trending, and know when the strategy should simply stay flat.
lessons.module_title: Module 4 — Knowing When to Stop, and the Playbook
lessons.html:
Every trend ends. That sounds obvious, but the pullback strategy has a particular weakness around trend endings, and it is worth facing directly: the last pullback of a trend looks almost exactly like every pullback before it. The market drifts back into the zone, the averages are still pointing the right way, and a perfectly respectable trigger candle appears. Then, instead of resuming, the trend rolls over.

You cannot avoid that entirely. What you can do is recognise the moment the trend is objectively over, stop looking for trades in its direction from that point, and recognise the conditions — ranges above all — in which the strategy should simply not be used. This lesson covers both.

The definitive signal: the structure break

Lesson 2 gave you a definition of an uptrend: higher highs and higher lows. The definition has teeth. An uptrend is over when price closes below the last confirmed higher low. A downtrend is over when price closes above the last confirmed lower high.

Two words in that rule do a lot of work.

Closes. A wick below the higher low that closes back above it is not a break. Markets routinely probe below obvious levels before turning back. The structure has held if the candle closes on the right side.

Confirmed. A higher low is only confirmed once price has gone on to make a new higher high after it (Lesson 2). A pullback low that has not yet been followed by a new high is a candidate, not a confirmed level. This matters, because it means the trend's invalidation level is often further away than the most recent low.

From the moment of that close, the pullback trader stops looking for longs. Not "reduces size", not "looks for stronger triggers": stops. The market may resume the uptrend later, but if it does, it will have to build new higher highs and higher lows first, and you will see it.

KEY POINT

An uptrend ends on a close below the last confirmed higher low. From that close, there are no pullback longs until a new uptrend is built.

The warnings before the break

The structure break is late by design. It waits for proof. Before it arrives, the market often gives earlier, softer warnings — the character changes Lesson 5 described. They do not end the trend, but they should make you more selective.

  • Shrinking impulses. Each push to a new high is shorter than the one before.
  • Deepening pullbacks. Pullbacks that used to stop at the 20 EMA now reach the 50, or beyond.
  • Flattening averages. The 20 and 50 EMAs lose their slope and start to converge.
  • Failure to make a new high. The latest rally stalls at or below the previous high — a "lower high in waiting".
  • Counter-trend muscle. The largest candles on the chart start pointing against the trend.

When two or three of these appear together, a sensible response is to take only the very best setups — strong confluence, clean trigger, ample reward — or to stand aside until the picture clears. When the structure break arrives, the question is settled.

After the break: the strategy can change sides

A broken uptrend is not automatically a downtrend. A downtrend needs its own credentials: a lower high and a lower low. Until both exist, the market is in no-man's-land, and the pullback strategy has nothing to offer on either side.

Once they do exist, the strategy simply turns around. The new downtrend has impulses and pullbacks of its own, and the first pullback into a lower high is a pullback sell under exactly the same rules.

Notice the order. The trader did not sell the break itself; that would be chasing in the opposite direction. They waited for the new trend to form its first lower high, then applied the full playbook: zone, trigger, stop beyond the swing, target at the recent low.

Ranges: where the strategy fails

The most expensive environment for a pullback trader is not a reversal. It is a range. Reversals at least end the argument with a clear structure break. Ranges keep the argument going for weeks.

A range is easy to describe once it is obvious: price oscillating between a ceiling and a floor, highs roughly equal, lows roughly equal, the moving averages flat and weaving through the candles. The trouble is that a range often begins looking exactly like a trend pausing. The first move down from the ceiling looks like a pullback. The bounce from the floor looks like a trigger. The trader buys — and the "new high" never comes.

How to recognise a range early

You do not need to wait for three touches of each boundary. Watch for these, in roughly this order:

  1. The trend fails to make a new extreme. After a pullback, the next rally stops at or just below the prior high. One equal high is a warning; two is a pattern.
  2. The averages flatten. The 20 EMA loses its slope and starts crossing the 50. Lesson 4's filter switches off.
  3. Pullbacks become symmetrical. The moves down are as large and fast as the moves up. Impulse and correction are no longer distinguishable.
  4. Triggers stop following through. Rejection candles appear, but the next few candles go nowhere.

When the first two appear together, the strategy is suspended. Not because a range cannot be traded — it can, with a different strategy — but because a pullback strategy in a range is a method buying the top of the floor and hoping for a ceiling that is not there.

COMMON MISTAKE

Reading equal highs as "the trend is just resting". A trend that has stopped making new highs has, for the moment, stopped trending. The strategy acts on what the structure is, not what it used to be.

A wick is not a break

The opposite mistake is declaring every trend over the moment price pokes below a level.

That chart contains a useful distinction. The trend's status and the setup's quality are separate questions. The trend survived, so a trader holding a long from earlier, with a structural stop below the higher low and a buffer, would still be in. But a new entry here, after a pullback of nearly the whole impulse, is poor value under Lesson 6's depth rule. Answer each question on its own.

Practice drill

Going deeper

Why closing-basis rules. Using closes rather than wicks costs you a little: a genuine break is recognised one candle later than an intrabar rule would show. In exchange, you avoid being shaken out by the probes below obvious levels that markets produce constantly. For a strategy whose stops already sit beyond the trigger, it is a good trade-off.

Timeframe matters, again. A structure break on H1 is a pullback on the daily chart more often than not. When the H1 trend breaks, the pullback strategy stops trading H1 longs. That says nothing about the daily trend, which may be offering a perfectly good pullback zone of its own a little lower. This is Lesson 9's alignment logic applied to endings.

Change of character versus break of structure. Some frameworks distinguish an early "change of character" (the first counter-trend break of minor structure) from a full break of the major trend structure. In plain terms: a lower-timeframe structure break is an early warning; a break of the trend timeframe's last confirmed swing is the verdict. You will see both terms used. The chart is the same either way — price first, framework second.

Hypothetical cost of range trading with a trend method. Suppose, illustratively, a trader keeps taking pullback trades through a three-week range and takes six trades: two reach 1R before reversing (closed at breakeven), four are stopped for −1R each. That is −4R in a period where the method's core assumption was false. The filter rules exist to prevent exactly this sequence — not by being clever, but by switching the strategy off.

Not every range is obvious in real time. You will sometimes take one or two trades at the start of a range before the evidence becomes clear. That is a normal, budgeted cost. The error is taking the fourth and fifth.

THE RULES
  • An uptrend ends on a candle close below the last confirmed higher low; a downtrend ends on a close above the last confirmed lower high.
  • After a break, take no trades in the old direction. Trade the opposite direction only after a new lower high and lower low (or higher low and higher high) exist.
  • Suspend the strategy when the trend fails to make a new extreme and the 20/50 EMAs flatten or cross.
  • A wick beyond the level that closes back inside is not a break — but the trend's status and the setup's quality are separate questions.

Summary

  • A trend ends on a close beyond its last confirmed swing; a candidate low that was never followed by a new high is not that level.
  • Softer warnings — shrinking impulses, deeper pullbacks, flattening averages — call for selectivity before the break arrives.
  • After a break, the strategy waits for a new trend to form, then can trade in the new direction from its first pullback.
  • Ranges are the strategy's most expensive environment; equal highs plus flat averages switch it off.
  • Wicks through a level are not breaks, but surviving the wick does not make a too-deep pullback a good entry.

lessons.title: Capstone — The Complete Pullback Playbook
lessons.summary: Run the whole strategy end to end — trend, pullback, zone, trigger, stop, target, size — on three full worked trades, including a loser, using the strategy passport and the pre-trade checklist.
lessons.module_title: Module 4 — Knowing When to Stop, and the Playbook
lessons.html:
You now have every piece. This final lesson puts them in order and runs them, start to finish, on three complete trades: two that work and one that does not. Then it gives you the two documents you will actually use day to day — the strategy passport, which fits the whole method on one page, and the pre-trade checklist, which you run before every single entry.

Nothing here is new. That is deliberate. A strategy you can trade is not a collection of clever ideas; it is a short sequence of plain questions answered honestly, in the same order, every time.

The playbook in ten steps

Before the session

  1. Choose your timeframes. One for trend and zone, one for the trigger, at a ratio of roughly four to six (Lesson 9). Write them down and do not change them mid-trade.
  2. Classify the trend on the higher timeframe using swing structure: higher highs and higher lows, lower highs and lower lows, or neither (Lesson 2). Confirm with the 20 and 50 EMAs (Lesson 4). Neither? Stop here for this market.
  3. Check for a range or an ending. Has the trend failed to make a new extreme? Are the averages flattening? Has a confirmed swing broken on a close (Lesson 10)? If so, stop.

When a pullback begins

  1. Judge the pullback's character. Slower and smaller than the impulse, mixed candles, last confirmed swing intact (Lesson 5)? If the counter-move is out-muscling the trend, stop.
  2. Mark the zone. The overlap of the 20–50 EMA band, the most recent broken swing level and the 38–62% retracement of the last impulse (Lesson 6). Write its edges down. Set an alert.
  3. Measure the reward in advance. From the middle of the zone to the prior high or low, against a stop beyond the zone. If it cannot reach 1.5R, the setup is unlikely to be worth taking.

When price reaches the zone

  1. Wait for a trigger on the lower timeframe: a rejection candle closing back in the trend direction, or a close through the pullback's own structure or line (Lesson 7). No trigger, no trade.
  2. Place the stop a small buffer beyond the trigger or the pullback extreme (Lesson 8). Never closer.
  3. Set the target — first target at the prior high or low, and decide in advance whether the rest runs to a measured move, a fixed R multiple or a trailing stop.
  4. Size the position so that a stop-out costs your fixed fraction of the account, illustratively 0.5–1%. Enter. Record the plan.
KEY POINT

Every step is a gate. A "no" at any of them ends the process. Most of the time, you will stop somewhere before step 7 — and that is the strategy working.

Worked trade 1 — the textbook long

An illustrative EUR/USD setup, trend and trigger both read from the four-hour chart to keep it simple.

Walking it through the steps:

  • Trend (2–3). Two higher highs and a confirmed higher low; the 20 EMA above a rising 50. No equal highs, no flattening. Trend confirmed.
  • Character (4). The impulse took about 20 candles to cover 117 pips; the pullback took 12 candles to give back about 55, with mixed colours and no large red candles. Healthy.
  • Zone (5). The 50% retracement of the impulse is roughly 1.0917; the 50 EMA is close by; the old high from the first leg, around 1.0890, sits just below. Zone: about 1.0906–1.0930.
  • Reward check (6). From the middle of the zone to the prior high at 1.0975 is roughly 55 pips. With a stop beyond the zone, comfortably above 1.5R.
  • Trigger (7). A pin bar with a 16-pip lower wick and a close in the top fifth of its range, inside the zone.
  • Stop (8). Three pips under the wick: 1.0904. Entry on the close at 1.0926. Risk 22 pips.
  • Target (9). T1 at the prior high, 1.0975 — 49 pips, about 2.2R. Half closed there, stop on the rest moved to breakeven; remainder aimed at the measured move, about 1.1025.
  • Size (10). Illustratively, 1% of a £10,000 account is £100; £100 ÷ (22 × about £7.50) ≈ 0.6 lots.

The trade reached T1 and later the measured move. The point is not that it won. The point is that every number was known before the trigger closed.

Worked trade 2 — a short in gold

The method is identical in a downtrend and on a different instrument. For gold the chart is in pips of 0.10, so a 300-pip move is 30 dollars.

  • Trend. Lower highs and lower lows; 20 EMA below a falling 50.
  • Character. The decline from 2374 to 2361 was fast and one-sided; the rally back is slower, with overlapping candles.
  • Zone. 50% of the last decline is about 2367.5; the 50 EMA is close; the old low at 2369 now sits just above as potential resistance. Zone: about 2366–2369.
  • Trigger. A bearish engulfing candle that swallows the previous green candle and closes near its low at 2365.8.
  • Stop. Above the engulfing high (2368.1) plus a buffer: 2368.6. Risk 2.8 dollars per ounce — 28 chart pips.
  • Target. Prior low at 2361.0, 48 pips away: about 1.7R. Above the 1.5R minimum, though not by a wide margin — a reason to take T1 in full rather than hope for more.
  • Size. Same £100 risk; the position is whatever size makes 28 pips on gold cost £100 on your platform. Gold's pip value differs from EUR/USD's; always calculate it, never assume.

Worked trade 3 — the loser

Losses are part of the method. Here is one, run by the same rules.

What went right: the trend was objectively up; the pullback was orderly and about 45% deep; the trigger was a genuine bullish engulfing in the zone; the stop sat beyond its low with a buffer; the prior high was about 1.9R away; the size was set for a 1% loss.

What went wrong: nothing that the rules could have caught in advance. The engulfing was followed by two weak candles and then a strong move down through the stop. Afterwards the market chopped sideways and never made a new high.

The trader's review should say exactly that: "Valid setup, valid execution, loss of 1R." It should not say "pin bars do not work", or "I should have used a wider stop", or "next time I will wait for two triggers". Changing rules after a single loss is how traders end up with a different strategy every week and no idea whether any of them work.

COMMON MISTAKE

Judging a trade by its outcome. A loss taken on a valid setup with the planned stop is a good trade. A win taken on a chased entry with no stop is a bad one that happened to work.

Reviewing your trades

Keep a simple record for every setup you consider, not only those you take. For each, note:

  • Date, pair, timeframes, direction.
  • Which gate it stopped at, or that it passed all ten.
  • Entry, stop, first target, R to first target, size.
  • Outcome in R, and a screenshot at entry and at exit.
  • One line: did I follow the plan? Yes or no.

After 30–50 recorded setups, look for patterns, not anecdotes. Do trades from deep pullbacks behave differently from shallow ones? Do structure-break triggers do better than pin bars for you? Are you consistently skipping steps on Friday afternoons? That evidence — not a single painful loss — is what earns a rule change.

A hypothetical illustration of why the record matters: suppose over 40 trades a trader averages +2.1R on winners and −1R on losers. With 14 winners and 26 losers, the total is 14 × 2.1 − 26 = +3.4R. With 12 winners it is −0.8R. The difference between those two outcomes is two trades out of forty. Without a record, nobody can tell which world they are in. These numbers are invented for illustration and say nothing about how the strategy will perform for you.

Final practice drill

The strategy passport

Everything above, on one page. Print it, or keep it next to your charts.

  • Market: liquid FX pairs and gold on H1 to D1, with confirmed higher highs and higher lows (or the reverse) and the 20 EMA above a rising 50 (or below a falling 50).
  • Wait for: a pullback slower and smaller than the impulse, reaching the 20–50 EMA band, the most recent broken swing level or the 38–62% retracement — ideally two of the three — while the last confirmed swing holds.
  • Trigger: a rejection candle (pin bar or engulfing) closing back in the trend direction from the zone, or a close through the pullback's own last swing or counter-trend line. Closed candles only.
  • Stop: a small buffer beyond the trigger or pullback extreme (default), or beyond the last confirmed swing (structural). Never in empty space.
  • Target: the prior high or low first; the remainder to a measured move, fixed 2–3R or a trailing stop beneath new swings. Minimum 1.5R to the first obstacle.
  • Size: a fixed fraction of the account per trade, illustratively 0.5–1%, calculated from the stop distance.
  • Avoid: ranges and flat or tangled averages; pullbacks that close beyond the last confirmed swing; counter-moves larger and faster than the impulse; higher-timeframe disagreement; major higher-timeframe levels inside 1.5R.

The pre-trade checklist

Run it before every entry. Every box must be ticked.

PRE-TRADE CHECKLIST
  • Higher timeframe shows higher highs and higher lows (or lower highs and lower lows) on confirmed swings
  • 20 EMA is on the correct side of the 50 EMA and both slope in the trend direction
  • The trend has made a new extreme recently — no equal highs or lows, no flattening averages
  • No candle has closed beyond the last confirmed higher low (or lower high)
  • The pullback is slower and smaller than the impulse before it, with mixed candles
  • The pullback has reached a zone where at least two of: 20–50 EMA band, broken swing level, 38–62% retracement overlap
  • The pullback has not retraced beyond about 79% of the impulse
  • A trigger has closed: rejection candle from the zone, or a close through the pullback's structure or line
  • Lower-timeframe trigger is in the higher timeframe's direction
  • Stop is beyond the trigger or pullback extreme, plus a buffer — not moved closer to improve the ratio
  • First target (prior high or low) is at least 1.5R away, with no major higher-timeframe level in between
  • Position size makes a stop-out cost the planned fraction of the account
  • Plan written down: entry, stop, T1, what happens to the remainder
THE RULES
  • Every step of the playbook is a gate; a "no" at any step means no trade.
  • Trend first, pullback second, zone third, trigger fourth — never out of order.
  • Stops come from the chart; size comes from the stop; targets must clear 1.5R to the first obstacle.
  • No trades in the old direction after a structure break; no trades in a range.
  • Judge trades by whether the plan was followed, not by their outcome. Change rules only on evidence from many recorded setups.

Going deeper

Make it yours, carefully. The rules in this course are a sound, conservative baseline. Over time you may want to adjust them: a different EMA pair, a tighter depth band, only structure-break triggers. Do it one change at a time, record at least 30 setups under the new rule, and compare like with like. Changing three things at once makes it impossible to know which one helped.

Market regimes. Trend strategies have seasons. During long ranging periods the strategy will produce few setups and several small losses; during strong trending periods it will produce many. Neither season tells you much on its own. Risk control is what lets you survive the quiet seasons to trade the good ones.

News and sessions. Major scheduled data can turn a perfectly good pullback into a spike through your stop in seconds. Many traders simply avoid new entries in the half hour around high-impact releases for the currencies they trade, and avoid holding very tight trigger stops through them.

What success looks like. Not a high win rate. A trader running this method well will typically lose on a meaningful share of trades, skip far more setups than they take, and make their results from the trades that run to 2R and beyond. If your records show you following the plan, keeping losses at 1R and letting winners reach their targets, you are doing it right — whatever the last five trades did.

Summary

  • The playbook is ten gated steps: timeframes, trend, range or ending check, pullback character, zone, reward check, trigger, stop, target, size.
  • Worked trades show the same logic long and short, on currencies and gold — and that a perfectly executed trade can still lose 1R.
  • Record every setup you consider, judge trades by plan adherence, and change rules only on evidence from many trades.
  • The strategy passport and the pre-trade checklist are your daily tools. Every box, every time.

options: At the entry
At one of the gates before the trigger — trend, ending, character, zone or reward
At the stop-loss
They should all be taken
quiz.why: Most markets most of the time fail at least one gate. Stopping early is the strategy working.

quiz.q: A setup passed every gate and lost 1R. What should the review say?
options: Pin bars do not work
Valid setup, valid execution, planned 1R loss
Use a wider stop next time
Double size on the next trade
quiz.why: Valid trades lose regularly. Changing rules after a single outcome destroys the evidence a record is meant to provide.

The reward to the first target is only about 1.7R — acceptable but not generous
Gold pips are worth more
Shorts must always use one target

options: First target at least 1.5R away
A trigger has closed
RSI is below 30
Position size set from the stop distance
quiz.why: The strategy uses structure, moving averages, retracement and candle triggers — no oscillator thresholds.

Change one thing, record at least 30 setups under the new rule, then compare
Stop using stops
Increase risk to recover faster
quiz.why: One change at a time, judged on a meaningful sample, is the only way to know whether the change helped.
